49: Building a tetrahedral 3D model that respects input boundaries exactly is computationally hard—adding extra points (Steiner points) at boundaries can corrupt the original topology. 50: Hologram phase patterns must encode the wavefront shape of a 3D scene to display it convincingly. The core problem is that traditional methods render light brightness separately from wave propagation, losing depth cues and reflection variety. By employing path tracing to collect both the brightness and the wave-optical field simultaneously, the method naturally encodes full 3D information into interference patterns. This is sound because both the rendering equation (measuring light) and the wave propagation equation (how waves combine) have the same underlying Monte Carlo solution structure—sampling paths and weighting by their contribution. A cache of ambient light further accelerates convergence, making physically accurate holograms practical.
51: Holographic displays use coherent laser light and special optical elements that distort color in complex, system-dependent ways. The core challenge is mapping user intent (desired colors) through all these transformations to achieve what the eye actually perceives. By modeling the full chain—input color space, display optics, and camera response (using learned neural models)—the system finds corrections at each stage. Adaptive illumination then tunes the laser intensity, reducing distortion further and making color fidelity achievable despite hardware imperfections.
52: Teaching a simulated character to move athletically is hard because pure motion copying lacks adaptability, while pure reinforcement learning loses natural motion quality. Parallel training with goal-conditioned rewards ties them together—the network learns when to follow reference and when to improvise, letting it replicate naturalness yet adapt to novel situations.
53: Creating full-color 3D holograms requires encoding three separate colors, which demands multiple optical elements or low efficiency. The core trick encodes only the real (amplitude) part of the interference pattern rather than both phase and amplitude, using shallower surface structures. A spatial frequency multiplexing strategy then separates the three colors by assigning each to different frequency bands, preventing them from interfering with each other. By inverting the collision detection logic (generating ground-truth collisions in exact arithmetic, then checking if algorithms find them), the method builds a rational benchmark revealing where floating-point implementations fail. 57: Creating volumetric graphics in air by exciting atoms with precisely timed laser pulses is inherently dim—one laser path cannot deliver enough photons fast enough. Using two synchronized laser paths working cooperatively concentrates photon delivery into a shared rendering volume, brightening the voxels significantly. 58: Seeing around walls using thermal radiation requires untangling how heat bounces off rough relay surfaces—the mixing is severe because rough surfaces scatter in many directions. A systems that learn from examples learns this convolution local rule directly from measurements rather than solving physics equations pixel by pixel. 59: Origami patterns fold into shapes with unusual stiffness—some directions resist bending while others do not, creating tailored mechanical properties. This is sound because crease geometry constrains how the sheet can bend and stretch—these constraints are deterministic and repeatable. 60: Large assemblies of jointed bodies become numerically fragile when you track object rotations directly, because rotation changes are nonlinear—a small conceptual change in orientation causes disproportionately large numerical swings. This paper's key insight is to separate motion into two pieces: a rigid body part (which moves linearly in a dual space of joint angles) and local shape deformations (which the method treats as nearly rigid). By working in this dual coordinate system where motion is linear, the underlying equation system stays well-conditioned, so you can reuse the same pre-computed solution structure across the entire simulation. This linear-in-dual-space property is mathematically sound because articulated bodies are constrained at their joints—those constraints eliminate most freedom and make the motion locally nearly rigid. Because the system structure stays constant, you can afford rule-based time stepping on huge numbers of bodies: the expensive setup is done once, not per step.
61: Human motion reuse across different body shapes fails when you copy limb positions directly: a tall person's reach and stride are fundamentally different from a short person's. The core problem is that motion semantics—the *intent* behind a movement—remain constant even though the positions don't. This paper models that invariance by learning which variations in position are "style" (acceptable changes that preserve intent) versus "core semantics" (the essential movement pattern). A learned model can separate these by seeing how the same intended motion changes across many real bodies. The method works because human motion has deep structure: intent creates tight correlations between joint angles and timings, so a model trained on many bodies learns to see through superficial position differences to the underlying pattern. This separation lets you then add user constraints (hold this hand at that position) while keeping the motion's fundamental character intact.
62: Relighting human performance frame-by-frame fails because skin surface appearance changes in complex ways when lights move: highlights slide, shadows cast by one body part onto another shift, and those local changes break temporal coherence. This paper learns a temporal model by capturing real relighting examples where the lighting changes smoothly over time and the performer moves naturally—data that shows how appearance truly changes. A learned generative model trained on such data learns the correlation structure: which appearance changes are physically plausible, and which violate how light actually behaves. The method works because video relighting isn't arbitrary—it follows the rules of how light bounces off skin and fabric. By representing each light source as a distinct learned concept (a pieces), the model can manipulate lighting independently and smoothly. Adding temporal consistency via attention over frames forces it to predict changes that don't contradict across shots, grounding outputs in real physics.
63: Feathers appear complex because their micro-structure—barbs and barbules—is organized hierarchically: they nest inside each other at finer and finer scales. The key insight is that all this detail follows a *single organizational pattern*: you can describe it procedurally (via rules for how barbs repeat and curve) rather than storing every strand. This works mathematically because natural feathers grew via biological rules that are continuous: small deformations at one scale smoothly propagate to the next. By reconstructing the hierarchical rules from one photograph (extracting the main curve and scale), you get a compact representation that lets you render at any zoom level—fine details appear where they're needed, coarse structure where you're far away. Self-shadowing and scattering follow naturally because the procedural description is geometric and continuous. This captures all visual realism of a feather while storing a tiny fraction of the data that an explicit detailed model would require.
64: Tracking dynamic scenes over long time periods fails because tiny errors accumulate: if you try to follow individual moving pieces through hundreds of frames, each piece drifts slightly, and by frame 200 everything is misaligned. The insight here is to think of motion as *local* rather than global—instead of asking where each piece goes, anchor pieces to a set of time-varying reference points (anchors) that only move slowly and smoothly. Each piece tracks only its *nearby* anchor, not the whole scene. This works because real scenes have coherent structure: nearby objects move together, and that coherence is more stable than tracking individual objects across long ranges. By only activating anchors relevant to the current frame and using multi-scale feature signals (global context plus local detail), the method keeps errors local and bounded. The mathematical soundness comes from treating motion as a composition of many small, locally stable transformations rather than one global deformation.
65: Reconstructing fluid flow from optical images requires inverting a high-dimensional measurement problem: light bends as it passes through the fluid, creating distorted images, and you must work backward to find which fluid density explains the observed distortion. The challenge is that this inverse problem is ill-posed—many different fluids could produce similar distortions. This paper organizes the high-dimensional data (a four-dimensional space-time volume) using a decomposition principle: instead of solving for all voxels at once, it breaks the four-dimensional structure into lower-rank pieces along different splitting planes. This reduces the problem size dramatically while keeping the essential information. The underlying principle is that fluid flow evolves smoothly in space and time, so the four-dimensional representation is *low-rank*—most variation comes from a few dominant patterns repeated across space and time. By decomposing along multiple planes and refining iteratively with a systems that learn from examples, the method leverages this structure to find an accurate reconstruction efficiently.
66: Liquid simulation with large time steps normally fails because particle motion becomes under-sampled: if you take a big leap in time, particles may jump over important flow features and miss wave crests or surface ripples, creating artifacts. This paper's key idea is to treat particles not as points in space but as samples spread over time: each particle occupies a small "slab" of four-dimensional space-time during each step. When depositing particles onto the grid, using a four-dimensional blur local rule naturally averages out aliasing that occurs from time-stepping jumps. This works because aliasing is a sampling problem—if you smooth across time as well as space during the averaging, you eliminate the high-frequency artifacts that would otherwise aliase into visible noise. The mathematical guarantee is that four-dimensional smoothing acts like a low-pass filter in the time direction, removing frequencies too fast to see. The method integrates seamlessly into standard liquid methods because it simply changes how particle contributions are spread, not the core physics.
67: Storing material appearance (how surfaces reflect light) compactly is hard because real materials have complex, high-dimensional variation—they scatter light differently depending on viewing angle and material roughness. This paper applies Bayesian statistics: rather than learning arbitrary values, it assumes appearance follows a smooth, probabilistic pattern (a prior belief that nearby measurements should be similar). Using a Bayesian approach means the model automatically balances fitting the measured data against staying smooth, avoiding overfitting. The specific choice of local rule (a distance-based covariance function) matches the actual structure of material properties—they vary smoothly, and this local rule captures that smoothness better than generic alternatives. The mathematical guarantee comes from Bayesian theory: the posterior is provably the best balance between data fidelity and simplicity given that prior. Adapting the input structure efficiently (organizing observations hierarchically) lets the method scale: the smoothness prior compresses what would otherwise be a massive table of measurements into a compact, analytic formula.
68: Reconstructing internal structure from sparse X-ray pictures is fundamentally ill-posed: thousands of different objects could cast the same shadows. But the problem becomes solvable if you constrain the search to only *known materials*—your interior must be made of one of a fixed set of elements. The method assigns each location a probability over which material lives there and minimizes a consistency loss: the assignment is good if, when you simulate X-rays passing through it, you recover the observed projections. This works because the physics of X-ray propagation is *deterministic and smooth*: small changes in material assignments produce small, predictable changes in what you'd measure. Optimizing via the downhill direction (working backward from measurement disagreement to material choices) is mathematically sound because this smoothness property means the downhill direction point toward better solutions. Treating each location as a probability (not a discrete choice) enables smooth optimization and naturally handles measurement ambiguity.
69: Computing whether a point is inside a closed surface is ambiguous for 3D models with holes, self-intersections, or tangled topology. The winding number is a topologically robust measure: it counts how many times the surface winds around the point. The key insight is to express winding number as two geometric pieces—ray intersections (straightforward to count) plus a boundary integral (the surface's projection onto an imaginary sphere around the point). This decomposition works because the sphere is a mathematical tool: the winding number theorem guarantees these two pieces sum to the correct answer *regardless* of how tangled the 3D model is. The efficiency gain comes from avoiding the integral: instead of integrating over the actual surface, you work with the discrete sphere projection, which has nice discretization properties. For 3D models, rays are simple geometry; for parametric surfaces, the projection is directly computable. The mathematical foundation—winding number theory—provides the guarantee that this decomposition is exact.
70: Covering a freeform architectural surface with flat panels requires balancing two competing goals: panels must align with the surface well (fidelity), and the assembled structure must resist bending and stress (strength). The paper models the panelization as a continuous surface that can creep like an elastic shell under stress: optimizing this continuous flow lets stresses feed back into the geometric choice. The method works because stresses have global structure—bending at one spot affects the whole surface's stability—so optimizing geometry and stresses together is sound. By representing each candidate panelization as a continuous surface instead of a discrete choice, the downhill direction can flow backward from stress measurements to shape changes. The objective integrates stress over the whole shell: minimizing this integrated quantity (rather than just local stresses) ensures the final design is globally robust, not patched locally. The continuous formulation makes optimization tractable on high-dimensional geometry.
71: 3D models self-intersect because local collision checks during simulation only stop parts from passing through their immediate neighbors—they don't prevent global tangling. Self-intersection is a global property: you can't fix it by moving one piece a millimeter. The paper's insight is to use two repulsive energies at different scales: a shape-level energy that sees the entire surface as one object and measures global entanglement, and a 3D model-level energy that prevents neighboring faces from crossing. The shape energy works because it measures geometric winding (using topological ideas like winding number)—this quantity smoothly captures whether the shape is knotted. The 3D model energy regularizes local interactions and provides the fine detail needed for practical untangling. Together they're sound because global embeddedness (no self-crossing) requires both preventing local collisions and fixing global tangles; neither alone suffices. The energy formulation ensures robust optimization: any configuration satisfying both energies is genuinely untangled.
72: Generating high-quality 3D shapes slowly is a known limitation of standard autoregressive and image-generating models: they need many sequential steps because each step is small. By predicting the next scale (finer level in the octree) rather than the next pieces, the model takes fewer, larger steps—each step commits to coarse decisions before refining. This works because octrees are inherently multiscale: parent nodes contain children, so choices at coarse scales constrain fine scales, and the model can exploit this structure via octree-aware attention. The mathematical advantage is that the search space at each step is smaller (you only choose among refinements of existing nodes), so fewer steps suffice to reach high fidelity. Speed comes from this structural leverage, not from doing less work overall.
73: Finding all curves where two parametric surfaces intersect is numerically fragile: small deviations in the search can miss tiny loops or confuse tangent touches for separate branches. The key is to robustly identify *all starting points* of intersection curves, even at degenerate spots. The paper uses winding number theory on a 2D vector field defined in the parameter space: the field represents surface normals projected onto each surface. Winding number counts how many times this field winds around a point—this count reveals isolated singularities and small loops that would confuse traditional searching. By subdividing the parameter space using this winding number test, the method robustly localizes starting points even where surfaces are tangent. The method works because winding number is a topological invariant—it's stable under small perturbations and detects features algebraic methods miss. Once starting points are located reliably, tracing intersection curves forward is straightforward.
74: Simulating thousands of yarn threads is computationally prohibitive because yarns interact through stretching, bending, twisting, and contact, creating a tightly coupled nonlinear system: changing one yarn's position affects neighbors through many coupled constraints. This transforms a brittle global solve into many robust local solves.

Each iteration brings the solution closer to equilibrium. The method is stable and empirically converges because the heat equation dampens errors, and the special spread of error reduction technique reduces Monte Carlo noise specifically at boundaries where it matters most.
85: Human motion is hierarchical: the body's center moves along a path while the limbs dance around it with their own detailed patterns. 87: The Walk on Spheres method solves equations by simulating random walks that bounce around inside a domain until they hit a boundary, then read off the answer. 89: A single microscope image of woven fabric contains only 2D visual information, yet you need to recover 3D fiber positions, orientations, and optical properties. The coarse-to-fine approach starts simple and adds detail as the estimate improves, avoiding local minima.

This approach works because phase fields obey fundamental smoothness and consistency properties: if you respect the field directions at every point and control thickness carefully, the resulting toolpaths automatically avoid clashing with previous layers and stay manufacturable, collapsing the many competing constraints into a single coherent geometric representation that can be solved directly.
92: Indoor scene generation faces a collision—enforcing building rules while avoiding mistakes from relating every object to every other object. This works because each stage conditions on outputs from the previous one, shrinking the search space and reducing the number of object-pair relationships to consider; the sparsity (only relevant semantic links, not fully connected) removes redundant error accumulation, and encoding the sparse graph into a compact space makes learning tractable, so each stage can focus on one geometric or semantic aspect rather than solving everything simultaneously.
93: Finding a one-to-one correspondence between two surfaces that minimizes distortion requires avoiding tangled or self-overlapping maps. Since the functional rewards flat, undistorted maps and punishes folds, the optimization is guaranteed to converge to bijections that preserve orientation—the mathematics of area minimization ensures injectivity emerges naturally without needing penalty terms or special initialization tricks.
94: Simulating stiff elastoplastic materials like clay or snow faces a stability wall: explicit time-stepping breaks into tiny pieces when materials resist compression, while rule-based methods struggle with the complex physics of flow and deformation. 95: Single-photon cameras count arriving light quanta one at a time—an extremely quantized, noisy measurement—yet the goal is to recover full-spectrum images. This works because the measurement process is unbiased (each detected photon is a fair sample of the incident spectrum) and independent; so long as you gather enough measurements, statistical law-of-large-numbers ensures the spectrum reconstructs accurately, and the error bound shrinks exponentially, making the approach sound despite the extreme quantization.
96: The medial axis—the set of all points equidistant from the boundary—describes shape by recording where spheres fit perfectly inside. 97: Virtual reality touch feedback typically requires expensive hardware or pre-built prop setups, but most real environments already contain objects with textures and weights. This works because semantic matching leverages learned world knowledge—large models understand which real materials feel like virtual ones—and the optimization balances competing criteria (size, reachability, haptic match) to find feasible proxies that deliver plausible tactile feedback without custom fabrication or active machinery.
98: Deforming 3D surfaces interactively requires both fitting detail and enabling direct manipulation without retraining. The approach uses a base subdivision surface (which has known, clean algebraic properties) plus an offset field learned via neural basis functions anchored to that base. This works because subdivision surfaces obey linearity, locality, and smoothness by design: any linear combination of control point displacements produces a proportional surface change, and the offset field inherits these properties through its base, so you can deform the 3D model directly via the control points without retraining while still capturing fine surface details in the learned offset.
99: Solving boundary-value equations on complex shapes requires either fine spatial discretization (expensive) or random walk simulation (slow and noisy). The hybrid approach splits the domain into small regular pieces, computes how random walks escape each piece (the Poisson local rule), then assembles these local escape probabilities into a large global equation and solves it exactly. This works because the spread of error of a random walk shrinks with domain size, so local escape probabilities are fast to estimate; replacing millions of walks with a single deterministic solve trades fast-to-compute random spread of error for controlled, reusable discretization error, getting geometric flexibility and parallelism from Monte Carlo while gaining speed and stability from the global solve.
100: End-to-end camera design must optimize optics for downstream processing (like image restoration), but a single-number loss function provides too few constraints for the hundreds of optical parameters, causing standard optimization methods to fail. The method lifts this scalar loss into ray-level residuals by measuring how rays deviate from perfect focus; now the high-dimensional residual vector feeds back into robust optimization methods designed for over-constrained problems. This works because ray-level measurements give rich directional information about which parts of the optical system cause problems, transforming an under-constrained scalar problem into a well-posed over-constrained one that standard second-order methods can handle reliably, bridging traditional optics tuning with modern end-to-end learning.
101: Virtual agents must move consistently with their role (hero, shadow, guide) and respond to the user's actions, requiring behavioral coherence across diverse situations. The system prompts a multimodal language model with scene layout, agent role, and user state to predict movement decisions and stylized paths.
